title: Slower Generalization, Faster Memorization: A Sweet Spot in Algorithmic Learning
claim: Convergence time does not fall monotonically with more data: for one task there is an intermediate dataset size that trains fastest, while another task shows no such slowdown.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared legend on top, log-log axes, solid vs dashed lines
description: Two log-log line plots sit side by side under a shared legend. The legend maps six colors, from dark navy to bright yellow, to exact-match thresholds τ from 0.1 to 0.98. Solid lines with square markers show validation crossings and faint dashed lines with dots show training crossings. Both plots put dataset size N on the x-axis and iterations to threshold on the y-axis. Panel (a), three-digit multiplication, shows validation curves that drop steeply and then flatten, with no late slowdown. Panel (b), NW matrix generation with L=5 and D=6, shows validation curves that fall, reach a minimum at intermediate N around 2k–4k, then rise sharply toward 100k. The training curves in (b) climb steadily and converge with the validation curves at large N. The eye goes first to the U-shaped dip in panel (b).
caption: Dataset-size sweeps for multiplication and NW matrix generation. Each curve reports the mean recorded number of optimizer updates needed to reach exact-match threshold \(\tau\); lower values mean faster convergence. Colors denote thresholds \(\tau\), solid lines show validation crossings \(I_V(\tau;N)\), and dashed lines show training crossings \(I_T(\tau;N)\). Multiplication shows no pronounced post-threshold slowdown. NW reaches validation thresholds fastest at intermediate sizes and more slowly at the largest dataset size in the sweep.
abstract: Once generalization becomes possible, does adding more data always make learning faster? In Needleman-Wunsch matrix generation, we find that small Transformers reach high exact-match validation accuracy in the fewest optimizer updates at an intermediate dataset size, while larger datasets converge more slowly. A random-suffix probe shows that, at larger dataset sizes, models fit the structured matrices before memorizing their random suffixes, suggesting that shared rule learning aids training-set fitting. To examine what makes rules easier to learn, we study elementary cellular automata (ECA), in which each binary cell updates from its own state and those of its two neighbors. These experiments identify lower-order predictive signals-output biases or predictive relationships involving only a few input bits-as a key factor in learnability. In Rule 90, finite-sample fluctuations create output biases and single-input dependencies absent from the uniform population. These signals weaken as the dataset grows. Biased training that introduces these signals accelerates generalization on an unchanged uniform validation distribution. These results support an explanation for faster convergence at intermediate dataset sizes: sampling fluctuations can facilitate rule acquisition, and larger datasets weaken this advantage.
